# Fintech Glossary

- **KYC (Know Your Customer):** Verifying a customer's identity before onboarding them.
- **AML (Anti-Money Laundering):** Rules and monitoring that detect and prevent illicit funds movement.
- **BaaS (Banking-as-a-Service):** Licensed banks expose their infrastructure via APIs so other companies can offer financial products.
- **Interchange:** Fee paid by the merchant's bank to the card issuer on each card transaction.
- **Open banking:** Customer-permissioned sharing of bank data with third parties via APIs.
- **ACH / RTP / FedNow:** US payment rails; ACH is batch and slower, RTP and FedNow are real-time.
- **PCI-DSS:** Security standard for handling card data.
- **Chargeback:** A customer-initiated dispute that reverses a card transaction.
- **Ledger:** The system of record for balances and transactions; must be accurate and auditable.
- **Unit economics:** Revenue and cost per customer or transaction; CAC, LTV, take rate.
- **Take rate:** The percentage of transaction volume the company keeps as revenue.
- **Underwriting:** Assessing the credit risk of a borrower.
- **SOC 2:** Audit report about a company's security and data controls.

> Tip: for each term, practice a one-sentence explanation a non-expert would understand.

suggestions.title: Campaign brief
suggestions.reason: One source of truth for goal, audience, messaging, owners and the week-by-week plan, built around the 14 Nov launch date

content.text: Launch content campaign: 6-week brief
Runs Mon 5 Oct to Sat 14 Nov 2026. The launch date moved to 14 November because the payments review slipped, so every deadline works back from that date.
Goal and targets
Primary goal: build a qualified pipeline for launch week (demo requests and trial signups).
Secondary goal: grow the email list and LinkedIn following before launch.
Targets: agree the numbers in week 1 and record them in the target fields on this desk.
Audience and messaging

Audience: decision-makers and day-to-day users at B2B companies who feel the problem our product solves. Draft the one-sentence value proposition, three proof points and the main objection with its answer here, then reuse them in every piece.
Owners (proposed)
Priya: campaign lead, launch date, demo video and final approvals.
Sam: content, press release, podcast and PR.
Alex: paid channels, tracking and analytics, budget and payments setup.
Week-by-week plan
Week 1 (5 Oct): foundations. Lock messaging, set up tracking and UTMs, publish the first thought-leadership post.
Week 2 (12 Oct): teaser. Announce something is coming, start the LinkedIn cadence and open the waitlist.
Week 3 (19 Oct): education. Publish how-to content and a customer problem story, and send the first nurture email.
Week 4 (26 Oct): proof. Release podcast episodes and early-access invites, and start paid retargeting.
Week 5 (2 Nov): momentum. Publish the demo video (due 5 Nov) and press release (due 7 Nov), and run the webinar.
Week 6 (9 Nov): launch push. Final countdown emails, partner posts, launch-day announcement on 14 Nov.
Risks and decisions
Risk: the payments review slips again. Mitigation: prepare a one-week-later version of the launch-week emails and posts.
Decision log: record each decision with a date and the person who made it.

suggestions.title: Japan trip overview
suggestions.reason: One brief with route, travelers, goals and a pre-departure checklist

content.text: Japan Family Trip - 14 Days
Four travelers, two weeks, one loop: fly into Tokyo, head to Hakone, then Kyoto and Osaka, and fly home from Osaka (KIX). Pace: one big thing per day, with downtime built in for the kids.
Route at a glance
Days 1-5: Tokyo (arrive Haneda/Narita, Asakusa, Shibuya, teamLab, day trip to Nikko or Kamakura)
Day 6: Hakone (onsen ryokan, Lake Ashi, Owakudani)
Days 7-10: Kyoto (Fushimi Inari, Arashiyama, Gion, Nara day trip)
Days 11-13: Osaka (Dotonbori, Osaka Castle, Universal Studios Japan)
Day 14: Fly home from Kansai International (KIX)
Family goals
Everyone picks 2 must-do things (log them in the Places wishlist)
Try at least one new food each day
Keep one slow afternoon every 2-3 days
Pre-departure checklist
Check all 4 passports are valid for the whole trip (6+ months is safest)
Register on Visit Japan Web for immigration and customs QR codes
Buy travel insurance for the whole family
Order pocket Wi-Fi or eSIMs
Tell banks about travel dates and get a no-foreign-fee card
Order yen cash for the first few days
Arrange luggage forwarding (takkyubin) between Tokyo and Kyoto

suggestions.reason: A draft 14-day plan to refine, with a task list per city

content.text: Itinerary (draft)
Tokyo - Days 1-5
Day 1: Arrive, get Suica/Pasmo cards, check in, easy walk and dinner nearby
Day 2: Asakusa and Senso-ji, Tokyo Skytree, Ueno Park
Day 3: Meiji Shrine, Harajuku, Shibuya Crossing, Shibuya Sky at sunset
Day 4: teamLab Planets, Odaiba, Ghibli Museum if tickets secured
Day 5: Day trip to Kamakura (Great Buddha, Enoshima) or Nikko
Hakone - Day 6
Romancecar from Shinjuku, Hakone Free Pass loop, ryokan with onsen and kaiseki dinner
Kyoto - Days 7-10
Day 7: Shinkansen to Kyoto, Gion evening walk
Day 8: Fushimi Inari early morning, Kiyomizu-dera, Nishiki Market
Day 9: Arashiyama bamboo grove, monkey park, Kinkaku-ji
Day 10: Nara day trip (deer park, Todai-ji), optional tea ceremony or kimono rental
Osaka - Days 11-13
Day 11: Osaka Castle, Umeda Sky Building, Dotonbori street food
Day 12: Universal Studios Japan (Super Nintendo World timed entry)
Day 13: Kaiyukan Aquarium, shopping, last-night family dinner
Departure - Day 14
Haruka express or limousine bus to KIX, tax-free souvenir stop, return IC card balances

content.text: Packing list (4 travelers)
Pack light: one carry-on plus one personal item each if possible. Hotels have laundry and Japan has coin laundromats, so plan for a week of clothes.
Documents & money
Passports x4 and printed copies
Visit Japan Web QR codes saved offline
Travel insurance details
Credit cards, yen cash and a small coin purse
Clothing
Layers appropriate to the season, plus a light rain jacket each
Comfortable broken-in walking shoes that slip on and off easily
Clean, hole-free socks (shoes come off at temples and restaurants)
Swimwear for onsen and hotel pools, and a modest outfit for shrines
Electronics
Phones, chargers and a 20,000mAh power bank
Type A plug adapter and a multi-port USB charger
Camera, spare memory cards, and eSIM or pocket Wi-Fi
Health & toiletries
Prescription medicine in original packaging (check Japan's import rules)
Pain relief, motion sickness tablets, plasters and blister pads
Sunscreen, deodorant and hand sanitizer
Day-to-day extras
Small towel or handkerchief (public restrooms often lack dryers)
Reusable bag and a zip bag for trash (public bins are rare)
Snacks and entertainment for the kids on long train rides
Empty space in the suitcase for souvenirs

data.title: Project Brief: Migrating the Team Wiki to PlexiiWrite

content.text: Purpose

Our team wiki needs a new home, and we have chosen PlexiiWrite. This brief sets out what the migration is meant to achieve, what is and is not included, how the work will be sequenced, and what could go wrong. It is a first draft for the project owner to refine before circulating.
Project owner:
[owner name]
Sponsor:
[sponsor name]
Target completion:
[go-live date]
Goals
The migration should leave the team with a wiki that is easier to use and easier to maintain than the one it replaces. Specifically, we want to:
Move all pages we decide to keep into PlexiiWrite with their content, structure and links intact.
Make sure people can find things quickly, through a clear page hierarchy and working search.
Retire the old wiki cleanly, so there is one source of truth and no one is left editing the wrong copy.
Give every team member enough orientation to start working in PlexiiWrite without a dip in productivity.

Success looks like this: the old wiki is read-only or decommissioned, the agreed content is live in PlexiiWrite, and the team is using it day to day. [Add any measurable targets, such as adoption or search success, if the team wants them.]
Scope
In scope:
An audit of the current wiki to decide what to migrate, archive or delete.
Mapping the existing structure to a page and space layout in PlexiiWrite.
Transferring content, including formatting, images, attachments and internal links.
Setting up access, permissions and ownership for each section.
A short guide and walkthrough for the team.
Redirecting or announcing the change so old links and bookmarks do not leave people stranded.
Out of scope, unless the sponsor decides otherwise:
Rewriting or substantially restructuring content beyond what the new layout requires.
Integrations with other tools beyond what already exists. [Confirm whether any integrations need to be rebuilt.]
Migrating content owned by teams outside ours.
Timeline
The plan runs in five phases. Dates are to be set once the owner confirms the go-live target and the size of the current wiki.
Audit and planning: inventory the existing pages, agree what moves, and settle the new structure. [start date to end date]
Pilot: migrate one representative section, check formatting, links and permissions, and note what the tooling gets wrong. [dates]
Full migration: move the remaining content in batches, with section owners checking their own pages. [dates]
Cutover: freeze edits on the old wiki, run a final sync, switch the team over and announce the change. [dates]
Follow-up: collect feedback, fix broken links, and decommission or archive the old wiki. [dates]
Risks

Content may not transfer cleanly. Tables, embedded media, macros and attachments often break between platforms. The pilot phase is there to find these problems early, and we should budget time for manual fixes.

Broken links. Internal links and external references to old page addresses may stop working. We should test links after each batch and keep the old wiki accessible in read-only form for a defined period.
Edits lost during cutover. If people keep editing the old wiki after the final sync, changes will be missed. A clear freeze date and a single announcement from the sponsor reduce this.
Low adoption. If people keep using the old wiki out of habit, the migration fails in practice. Short training, visible leadership use and a firm retirement date help.
Permissions set incorrectly. Sensitive pages could become too open or too restricted. Each section owner should confirm access before go-live.
Unclear ownership. Pages with no owner decay quickly. Every section should leave the migration with a named owner.
Next Steps
Confirm the owner, sponsor and go-live date.
Start the content audit and share the keep, archive or delete list for review.
Schedule the pilot migration.

data.title: Support Agent Onboarding Guide: Your First Week

content.text: Welcome

Welcome to the support team. This guide covers what your first week looks like, the tools you will use, and how we handle escalations. It is a starting point, not a rulebook you need to memorize. Your onboarding buddy, [buddy name], and your manager, [manager name], are the people to ask when something here is unclear or out of date.
By the end of the week, you should be comfortable working your own queue with support from teammates, know where to find answers, and know exactly when and how to hand a case to someone else.
What to Expect This Week
The week moves from observing, to working with guidance, to handling tickets on your own. The pace may shift depending on how the queue looks, and that is fine.
Day 1: Setup and orientation

Get your accounts and access sorted, meet your buddy and the wider team, and read through this guide. Your manager will walk you through team goals and how your work is measured. Spend any spare time reading recent resolved tickets to get a feel for our tone and the kinds of questions customers ask.
Days 2 and 3: Shadowing and learning the product

Sit in on live work with experienced agents, whether that means reading over their shoulder on tickets or listening to calls, depending on the channels we cover. Use the product yourself as a customer would. Try to reproduce common issues so you understand them firsthand. Start a personal notes document of questions, terms and answers you look up more than once.
Day 4: Handling tickets with review

Begin answering real tickets from a limited queue. Your buddy reviews your replies before or soon after they go out. Expect feedback on accuracy, tone and clarity. This is normal for everyone and is not a judgment of your ability.
Day 5: Working independently, with a check-in
Take a fuller share of the queue. At the end of the day, meet with your manager to talk through what went well, what felt hard, and what to focus on in week two. Bring your list of open questions.
Your Tools
You will be given access to the tools below. Exact products and logins are listed in the access checklist from your manager, so treat this section as a map of what each category is for.
The helpdesk or ticketing system, where customer conversations are received, assigned, tracked and closed. [helpdesk tool name]
The internal knowledge base, where approved answers, troubleshooting steps and policies live. [knowledge base tool name]
Team chat, for quick questions, handoffs and staying in touch with colleagues. [chat tool name]
The admin or account lookup tool, for viewing customer account details needed to resolve issues. [admin tool name]
The bug or issue tracker, where product problems are reported to engineering. [issue tracker name]

A few habits will serve you well with all of them. Search the knowledge base before asking a colleague, and if you find it wrong or incomplete, flag it so it gets fixed. Keep ticket notes clear enough that someone else could pick up the case without asking you anything. Only access customer account data when you need it to help that customer.
How We Communicate With Customers

Write the way you would want to be written to. Acknowledge the problem, say what you are doing about it, and be honest about what happens next. Avoid jargon the customer has not used themselves. If you do not know the answer, say so and tell them when they will hear back, then follow through on that promise.

Never guess at an answer to look helpful. A short, accurate reply that says you are checking is better than a confident wrong one. Our response and resolution targets are [response time targets], and your manager will explain how they apply to each channel.
How We Handle Escalations

An escalation is a handoff of a case to someone with more expertise, authority or access than you have. Escalating is a normal part of the job. It is not a failure, and a well-made escalation is a sign of good judgment.
When to escalate
Consider escalating when any of these apply:
You have checked the knowledge base and tried the standard steps, and the issue is still unresolved.
The problem looks like a bug or outage rather than a usage question.
The customer is requesting something outside your authority, such as a refund beyond your limit or an exception to policy. [your approval limits]
There is a security, privacy or legal concern, including anything involving a data request or a suspected account compromise.
The customer is very upset, has raised the issue repeatedly, or has asked for a manager.
You are unsure. Asking early is always better than letting a case sit.
How to escalate
Before you hand a case off, make sure the receiving person can act without going back to the customer for basics. A good escalation includes:
A short summary of the issue and what the customer wants.
The customer and account details relevant to the case.
Steps you have already tried and what happened.
Any screenshots, logs, error messages or reproduction steps.
The urgency and why, including any deadline the customer has mentioned.

Post the case through [escalation channel or process], and assign it to the right team: [escalation tiers and owners]. Then tell the customer what you have done. Let them know the issue has been passed to a specialist, what to expect, and roughly when they will hear back. Do not leave a customer waiting in silence while the case moves internally.
After you escalate

You still own the customer relationship until the case is formally handed over and the other party has accepted it. Check in on the case at sensible intervals, keep notes updated, and make sure the customer gets an update even if the news is that work is still in progress. When the case is resolved, read the outcome. It is one of the fastest ways to learn.
Urgent and critical issues

Some situations cannot wait for the normal process, such as a widespread outage or a serious security concern. In those cases, follow the urgent path: [urgent escalation contact or on-call process]. If you are not sure whether something qualifies, treat it as urgent and ask.
Working With Your Team

You will learn fastest by asking questions and sharing what you find. Use team chat for quick questions, and do not wait until you are stuck for hours. Share useful discoveries, and if you handle a tricky case well, consider writing it up for the knowledge base. Regular one-to-ones with your manager are at [meeting cadence], and your buddy is your first stop for day-to-day questions.
First-Week Checklist
Accounts and access are working for every tool on your list.
You have met your buddy, your manager and your immediate teammates.
You have read this guide and the key knowledge base articles your manager points you to.
You have used the product as a customer would.
You have handled at least a few real tickets with review.
You know when to escalate, how to do it, and where to post it.
You have a list of questions for your end-of-week check-in.
Who to Ask
Day-to-day questions: [buddy name]
Priorities, performance and anything about your role: [manager name]
Access and tooling problems: [IT or tools contact]
Urgent or critical issues: [urgent contact]
Welcome again. Nobody expects you to know everything this week. What we ask is that you stay curious, ask early, and take care of the customer in front of you.

data.title: How to Write a Good Bug Report

slides.title: How to Write a Good Bug Report
slides.notes: Welcome everyone. This session is about a small skill that saves a lot of time: writing a bug report that someone else can act on without asking you questions. We will cover why it matters, what to include, and how to check your own work.

slides.title: Why a good report matters
bullets: The reader was not there when it happened
Missing details cause back-and-forth and delay
A clear report gets fixed sooner and more accurately
A vague report can get closed as 'cannot reproduce'
Your goal is that anyone can pick it up cold
slides.notes: Frame the report as a handoff. The developer or tester reading it has none of your context. Every question they have to ask is a delay, so the best report answers those questions before they are asked.

slides.title: The anatomy of a useful report
bullets: A short, specific title
Steps to reproduce, numbered and in order
Expected result
Actual result
Environment: version, device, browser, account type
Evidence: screenshot, recording, logs or error text
slides.notes: Walk through each part in order. The title should name the problem, not just the area. Steps should be exact enough that a stranger can follow them. Expected versus actual is what makes it clear why this is a bug at all.

slides.title: Weak versus strong, side by side
bullets: Weak title: 'Checkout broken'
Stronger title: 'Checkout button does nothing after applying a discount code'
Weak step: 'Try to pay'
Stronger step: '3. Click Pay now with a valid code applied'
Weak result: 'It fails'
Stronger result: 'No response, and no error message appears'
slides.notes: Use these examples to show the difference in specificity. Then invite the group to suggest their own weak report from experience and rewrite it together. Keep it light; the point is to practice the habit.

slides.title: Make it reproducible and focused
bullets: Try it again before you file it
Note whether it happens every time or only sometimes
Cut steps that do not affect the result
One bug per report
Check for an existing report first
State the impact, such as who is affected and how badly
slides.notes: Reproducibility is the most valuable thing you can add. If it is intermittent, say so and describe what you tried. Keeping one bug per report makes tracking and fixing much simpler, and a quick search for duplicates saves everyone effort.

slides.title: Your pre-submit checklist
bullets: Could a stranger follow my steps?
Are expected and actual results both stated?
Is the environment listed?
Is there evidence attached?
Is the tone factual and blame-free?
slides.notes: Close by asking everyone to run this checklist before they hit submit. Keep the tone neutral and about the product, never the person who built it. Encourage the team to use this on the next bug they file, and to share good examples in [team channel or tracker name].

verdict.reason: The summary accurately reflects the document's key findings (browser dominance, no culling, thresholds, wire/minimap hot paths) and gives the three recommendations P1-P3 in the document's priority order, with no invented content.

results.text:
## Key Findings

- **Browsers dominate memory.** Each browser is a full Chromium renderer process that never sleeps, using roughly 80 MB for a light page and 150-400 MB for heavy SPAs. Only the active desk is mounted, so cost depends on how many widgets sit on that one desk.
- **There is no viewport culling.** Every widget on the active desk stays fully mounted and live, whether it is on screen, panned away, or hidden. This makes compositing and pan/zoom jank worse on browser-heavy desks.
- **Risk climbs steeply with browser count.** Up to 3 browsers is comfortable; 9-15 causes real swap pressure and jank; 16+ risks renderer kills and blank browser widgets.
- **Live wires and the minimap are the main CPU hot paths.** Wire overlay does O(wires) DOM reads per frame during drags, and the minimap re-renders every widget as a live preview on each layout change. Both become noticeable at roughly 30-50+ wires or dense desks.
- **Other widgets are cheap.** Most non-browser widgets cost under 30 MB each, and portals are inexpensive because they render static miniatures.

## Top 3 Recommendations

1. **Suspend offscreen and hidden browsers.** Use an IntersectionObserver or pan/zoom-driven visibility check in `WebViewWidget` to mute, throttle, or unload browsers that are fully off screen or occluded, reloading them when they return. This addresses the biggest stability risk and the compositor jank.
2. **Viewport-cull the canvas.** Skip mounting widgets well outside the viewport, with a margin, so large desks only mount what is near view. Browsers benefit most.
3. **Warn when a desk holds many browsers.** Track the live webview count and show a gentle performance hint past roughly 8 browsers per desk, which is cheap to add and prevents the worst surprises.

It is not a second edition and not a place to keep a workspace [1]. It runs the same renderer and data layer as the desktop, compiled to WebAssembly [1]. Sharing between existing users and within organisations stays on the desktop, with two-way sync [1].

**Why differences exist:** Each is **Cannot** (a browser can't do it), **Chosen** (we decided against it, usually for safety) or **Not yet** (ordinary remaining work) [1].

**Main differences:**
- No sign-in, orgs, or own workspace, and no two-way sync from a shared desk. A recipient's copy is a snapshot that reaches nobody [1].
- Most of the 46 widgets behave identically. Some are partly limited (e.g. markdown export, AI regeneration, CSV import) and some are unavailable: streamdeck and local-app-launcher (Cannot), agent (Chosen), image-gen, webhook, inbound-hook and attention (Not yet) [1].

- The Vault is always locked (Not yet, because its crypto is synchronous) [1].
- BYOK is Anthropic only, with the key held server-side [1].
- PlexiBrain semantic search and memory extraction from documents are unavailable (Chosen), and sending AI chat messages is not served yet [1].
- Working fine: drive, offline use, multiple tabs, AI via credits, calendar, focus tools and notifications [1].

**Coverage:** The browser serves 197 of the desktop's 529 channels. A full session of sign-up, desk creation, editing, upload and sharing needs only one missing channel, `mail:getAccount`, which cannot exist in a browser [1].

results.prompt: Summarise the decision this ADR makes and the main risks it lists.

verdict.reason: The summary states the phased hybrid decision, the rejection of Option B and the phase details accurately, and lists all five ADR risks with mitigations, with nothing invented and a sensible, concise scope that leaves out the unrelated DRM addendum.

results.text:
**Decision:** Adopt a phased hybrid rather than replacing the browser wholesale. The browser is already real Chromium (`<webview>`), and the login failures came from fixable defects, chiefly a missing User-Agent [1]. The phases are: (1) harden `<webview>`, which is shipped and proven: clean UA, overlay `setActive` instead of `focusOn`, origin-gated autofill, and a permission denylist; (2) an external-browser OAuth handoff (`shell.openExternal` plus `haptyx://` and `session.cookies.set`/PKCE) for providers that block embedded browsers; (3) a native `WebContentsView` scoped to the focus/expand surface, with `session.loadExtension` for uBlock-Lite and Dark Reader; (4) screenshot-at-rest plus one pooled native view on activate, gated behind a spike. Phases 2-4 are proposed [1]. Option B, a wholesale native `WebContentsView` migration, is rejected because it would sacrifice smooth pan/zoom, clipping and layering [1].

**Main risks listed:**
- The UA regex could mangle the version string. This is mitigated by unit tests and idempotence [1].
- Some enterprise SSO blocks embedded browsers regardless of UA. Only Phase 2 fixes those; Phase 1 narrows the failures but does not eliminate them [1].
- Phase 4's native-view/CSS-transform sync is make-or-break. It needs a spike proving 60fps pan/zoom tracking and acceptable clipping; if the spike fails, stop at Phase 3 [1].
- The origin gate may be too strict for edge-case login domains. It fails closed, so autofill simply doesn't fire [1].
- Extension security: use a vetted shelf only, load specific reviewed builds, never arbitrary user-supplied extensions, and document the supported-API subset [1].

The extensions caveat is also stressed: Electron supports only a subset of the Chrome API, so the product should promise a vetted shelf, never Web-Store parity [1].
